tip: There's no word for 'let's' in French – the -ons ending carries it. Partageons = 'let's share'. Any nous-form verb becomes a suggestion this way.
French 'has' confidence rather than being confident: avoir confiance en = to trust. Ayez confiance en vous = have faith in yourselves.
The 'il' in il va pleuvoir is a placeholder, not a person – like the 'it' in 'it's raining'. Weather verbs like pleuvoir never take a real subject.
'What's wrong' is literally 'what isn't going': ce qui ne va pas. The verb aller (to go) doubles as 'to be OK' – ça va = it's going/fine.
No question word needed – just a rising tone and a '?'. Tu as reçu mon message ? is a full yes/no question, same words as the statement.
'Before' + an action needs 'de' plus the plain verb: avant de jouer = before playing. French uses the infinitive where English uses the -ing form.
'Affaires' isn't 'affairs' – it means your things or belongings. Rangez vos affaires = put away your stuff.
'L'addition' is the restaurant bill, not a maths sum. Je paierai l'addition = I'll pay the bill. You ask for it with 'L'addition, s'il vous plaît'.
French has no separate '-ing' tense: je te parle means both 'I talk to you' and 'I'm talking to you'. Context tells you which.
French uses 'the' for body parts, not 'your': Donne-moi la main = give me your hand (literally 'the hand'). The owner is already obvious.
In everyday French 'on' means 'we': on est pressés = we're in a hurry. It takes a singular verb (est) even though it means us.
After 'quand' French uses the future where English uses the present: quand nous aurons économisé = 'when we've saved'. Both clauses stay future.
'Chez' means 'at someone's place' in one word: chez des amis = at friends' house. No English equivalent – it always points to a person's home or shop.
French doesn't 'need' – it 'has need of': avoir besoin de. Tu auras besoin de ton passeport = you'll need your passport. Always followed by de.
'Offrir' means to give as a gift, not to 'offer': lui offrir un livre = to give him a book. A present is always offrir, never donner.
'Avaient essayé' is the 'had done' past – one step further back than a past event. They had already tried several places before finding le bon (the right one).
